metadata.title: Central limit theorem: the means, not the raw data, turn bell-shaped
metadata.subject: Statistics
metadata.objective: Show sample means becoming more normal and less variable as sample size grows.
misconceptions: The raw data becomes normal as n grows
A larger n increases the standard error
metadata.expectedUnderstanding: The left panel is the parent population and it never changes, however large n gets. The right panel is the distribution of the sample mean: as n grows its spread shrinks like sigma over the square root of n (so quadrupling n halves the standard error) and its shape approaches the normal curve. The approach is a limit: at finite n the drawn bars stay slightly skewed, and no exact normality is claimed.

primitives.text: Central limit theorem: the means, not the raw data, turn bell-shaped
standard error of the mean (red bar): shrinks as n grows

checkpoints.prompt: Two panels are on screen. Which one shows the raw observations, and which one shows the distribution of the sample mean?
n is now 10. Compare the right-hand bars with the n = 3 start: did their spread grow or shrink?
Continue to n = 30 and watch the middle bars: does the shape get closer to the dashed curve?
At n = 60 the bars still sit slightly off the dashed curve. Is the distribution of means exactly normal at finite n, and if n goes from 9 to 36, what happens to sigma over the square root of n?

narration.text: On the left are the raw observations: one skewed population, and it does not change however large the samples get.
On the right is a different quantity, the sample mean. Each bar is the chance that a sample mean falls in that slice.
Now raise n. Every mean is still drawn from that same skewed population on the left.
At n = 10 the outer bars have already fallen toward the middle: the spread of the means is smaller than at n = 3.
At n = 30 the shape tracks the dashed normal curve closely, and the standard error, sigma over the square root of n, has roughly halved since n = 3.
At n = 60 the red standard-error bar is about a fifth of its starting length: quadrupling n halves the standard error, it never increases it.

fallback.text: Static two-panel figure. Left panel: the skewed parent population as four bars of height 200, 132, 84, 52 over a common baseline, labelled raw data and never redrawn. Right panel: five schematic bars for the distribution of the sample mean at three sample sizes, drawn as three stacked rows with the same horizontal bins. Row n = 3: heights 46, 34, 30, 22, 14 (flat and right-skewed, standard error 3 over the square root of 3 = 1.73). Row n = 10: 33, 41, 63, 62, 24 (standard error 0.95). Row n = 60: 30, 84, 132, 86, 32 (standard error 0.39, dot-dashed normal curve overlaid). A caption reads: the left panel is the fixed parent population, the right panel is the mean of n draws; the spread falls as 1 over the square root of n and the shape approaches normal as a limit, not exactly at any finite n.

accessibility.alt: Two histograms on a shared baseline with no vertical axis. The left one, labelled raw data (parent), is skewed: four bars descending from tall on the left to short on the right, and it never moves. The right one, labelled sample means, has five blue bars under a dashed grey bell curve; as n rises from 3 to 60 the outer bars shrink, the middle bar grows, and the bar shape tightens onto the dashed curve. Under the right panel a red horizontal bar labelled standard error shrinks from about 150 to about 34 pixels as n rises.
accessibility.reducedMotion: Show three static rows of the right-hand histogram side by side, n = 3, n = 10 and n = 60, over the same bins and under the same dashed curve, with the standard-error values 1.73, 0.95 and 0.39 printed under each row and the unchanged left panel reproduced beside them.
